t: 3448. Count Substrings Divisible By Last Digit
o: For every substring we look at its last (non-zero) digit d and ask whether the whole substring's numeric value is divisible by d. In "12936", 11 of the 15 substrings qualify. Brute force checks each of the O(n²) substrings, but n can be 1e5, so we need to count, for each ending position, how many prefixes ending there have remainder 0 modulo the last digit — a classic digit DP over remainders for divisors 1..9.
k: Only the last digit matters, and it is one of 1..9, so we maintain remainder counts modulo each d simultaneously.
When appending digit c, every existing remainder r transforms to (r·10 + c) mod d — an O(1) update per (d, r) pair.
Leading zeros are harmless: the DP tracks raw numeric remainders, so "01" is handled correctly.

a.i: Fix the end index and extend the start leftwards, maintaining the value modulo 2520 (= lcm of 1..9) so divisibility tests are O(1). Clear and correct, but O(n²) — too slow for n = 1e5, yet perfect for explaining the problem.
s: For each end i, keep running remainder r starting at 0.
For each start j moving left to right, update r = (r·10 + digit) mod 2520.
If digit s[j] is non-zero and r mod digit == 0, count the substring.
a.t: O(n²) — quadratic pair scan; TLE at n = 1e5

a.i: Keep cnt[d][r] = number of substrings ending at the previous character with value ≡ r (mod d). On reading digit c, each count moves to remainder (r·10 + c) mod d, and the length-1 substring contributes one count at c mod d. The substrings ending here that are divisible by their last digit c are exactly cnt[c][0] afterward. Total work is 81 operations per character.
s: For each character c: build new counts by shifting old remainders, add the singleton at c mod d, and if c > 0 add new[c][0] to the answer.
Replace cnt with the new table and continue.
a.t: O(81·n) — constant 9×9 remainder updates per character

w: Lead with the brute force to show understanding, then pivot to the DP when asked about n = 1e5. Key correctness points: the last digit determines the divisor, so we only read cnt[c][0] when the current char is c; digit '0' endings never count (division by zero excluded by the problem). Edge cases: strings of all zeros return 0; single non-zero digits always count. Watch for 64-bit answer types — up to ~5·10⁹ substrings.
